chunks: Short-circuiting a LiPo. The question: What happens when you short circuit a LiPo?
A LiPo cell has very low internal resistance, only milliohms. So if you connect its terminals directly with a wire, the current is huge.
Only that small internal resistance limits it. All of that current heats the cell and the wiring, and it can lead to venting and fire within seconds.
Protection has to be fast and built in.
Picture a full water tank whose only outlet is a short, very wide pipe.
Open it straight to the outside and the water rushes out, held back only by that pipe, which barely slows it.
The cell's internal resistance is that pipe: it is tiny, so the current is enormous.
The picture breaks in one way that matters: spilled water just makes a puddle, while the battery's current turns into heat inside the cell itself.
The only things limiting the current are R int and R ext . A fuse in series is the intended last resort. The animated flow shows the short loop.
Short circuit: a direct low-resistance path across the battery terminals. Internal resistance: the cell's own resistance, usually milliohms ("Battery internal resistance").
Ohm's law: I equals V over R , so a small resistance gives a large current. I²R heating: heat equals current squared times resistance.
Fuse / protection IC: parts that cut the circuit quickly when current is too high ("Why charging and monitoring ICs matter").

"A LiPo has milliohm-level internal resistance, so a short is limited almost only by that: one 4.
2 volts cell at 50 milliohms gives about 84 amps, and a 4S hobby pack with 20 milliohms gives around 840.
That puts hundreds of watts to kilowatts of I to the 2R into the cell and wiring, heating it by many degrees per second toward venting and thermal runaway.
So you need layered protection: a properly rated fuse, a fast short-circuit-detecting protector IC, cell-level devices, and wiring and connectors that prevent shorts."
